issues.legal_issue: The Chief Settlement Commissioner may cancel an allotment of land exceeding the allottee’s statutory entitlement even after proprietary rights have been granted.
material_facts: The allottee received land in excess of the area to which he was entitled.
Proprietary rights had been granted in respect of the allotments before the excess was detected.
The Chief Settlement Commissioner set aside the Managing Officer’s order permitting purchase of the excess land.
issues.conclusion: The Chief Settlement Commissioner was competent under section 24 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, to cancel the excess allotment, notwithstanding the grant of proprietary rights.
issues.legal_principle: Section 24 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, empowered the Chief Settlement Commissioner to cancel an allotment exceeding the allottee’s entitlement. The Court approved the principle in Smt. Balwant Kaur v. Chief Settlement Commissioner (Lands), Punjab, that an order of transfer could be cancelled even after a sanad had been granted or a sale deed executed, with the instrument falling with the cancellation.

predicates.appeal_from_excess_allotment_cancellatio: The proceeding is an appeal challenging cancellation of an excess land allotment.
predicates.allotment_exceeded_entitlement: The allottee received more land than the applicable entitlement allowed.
predicates.proprietary_rights_were_granted: The allottee had been granted proprietary rights in the allotted land.
predicates.chief_settlement_commissioner_can_cancel: The Chief Settlement Commissioner can cancel the allotment to the extent it exceeds the allottee’s entitlement.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges cancellation of an excess allotment, an allotment beyond the recipient’s entitlement may be cancelled even if proprietary rights had been granted.

issues.legal_issue: A central rehabilitation authority cannot authorize the sale of excess land after that land has been transferred out of the central compensation pool to the state government.
material_facts: The excess land was transferred to the state government under a package deal effective before the Managing Officer’s sale order.
The Managing Officer permitted the allottee to purchase the land after that transfer.
The land was no longer part of the central compensation pool when the Managing Officer made the order.
issues.conclusion: The Managing Officer’s order permitting purchase was wholly without jurisdiction because the land had vested in the state government and was no longer in the central compensation pool.
issues.legal_principle: The package deal transferred the relevant property from the Central Government to the state government, so settlement authorities acting as delegates of the Central Government could not make orders concerning it under the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954. The Court approved Ram Chander v. State of Punjab, whose ruling on the validity and effect of the package deal had been upheld by this Court.

predicates.appeal_challenges_central_sale_order: The proceeding is an appeal challenging an order by a central rehabilitation authority permitting a sale.
predicates.land_transferred_to_state_before_sale_or: The land had been transferred to the state government before the authority made the sale order.
predicates.land_outside_central_compensation_pool: The land was no longer held in the central compensation pool when the sale order was made.
predicates.central_rehabilitation_authority_lacks_p: A central rehabilitation authority lacks power to authorize the sale of land that has vested in the state government.

issues.definition: A central rehabilitation authority cannot authorize a sale when the proceeding concerns its sale order and the land had already left the central compensation pool and transferred to the state.

issues.legal_issue: The state government must determine whether an allottee’s legal representatives may purchase cancelled excess land under the applicable state disposal rules.
material_facts: The deceased allottee’s legal representatives sought to purchase the cancelled excess land.
The land had become package deal property vested in the state government.
The Punjab Package Deal Properties (Disposal) Rules, 1976, provide a procedure for transferring cancelled excess land to allottees or their successors-in-interest.

The rules exclude entitlement to the excess land where its cancellation was based on fraud, concealment, or misrepresentation of material facts, and provide for a price based on current market value determined by the Tehsildar (Sales).
issues.conclusion: The state government must consider and decide whether the legal representatives are entitled to purchase the excess land under the applicable state legislation and rules; the Court did not itself determine their eligibility.
issues.legal_principle: Under the Punjab Package Deal Properties (Disposal) Act, 1976, and the Punjab Package Deal Properties (Disposal) Rules, 1976, the state government considers transfers of cancelled excess land to allottees or successors-in-interest. Rule 4 excludes entitlement where cancellation was for fraud, concealment, or misrepresentation of material facts, and clause 8 provides for the current market price to be determined by the Tehsildar (Sales).

predicates.appeal_concerns_cancelled_package_land: The proceeding concerns excess land cancelled after it became property held by the state government under a package transfer.
predicates.legal_representatives_seek_to_purchase_l: The former allottee’s legal representatives seek to purchase the cancelled land.
predicates.state_government_must_determine_successo: The state government must determine the successors’ purchase eligibility under the applicable disposal rules.

issues.definition: When legal representatives seek to purchase cancelled package land, the state government determines their eligibility under the applicable disposal rules.
